You are picking up a **custom C++20 + Vulkan voxel sandbox** built from scratch. Not a mod, not Unity — a real engine. This page exists so you are useful in ten minutes instead of an hour.

**It is no longer short, and that is deliberate — §3 is the whole state of the project.** Use the index above: §1 and §2 are the ones nobody may skip, §3 is a reference to dip into, and §4 onward are answers to specific questions. If you read nothing else, read §1 and the box at the top of `CLAUDE.md`.

---

## 0. The sixty-second version

- **Milestones 1–29 are done** (plus M29b–m). The game is genuinely playable: an endless seeded world, survival, combat, farming, villages, 57 creature species, a deferred HDR renderer with shadows, clouds, weather and water reflections. **M30, hardware ray tracing, is next and is optional.**
- **No fault is currently open.** The last round closed on 2026-08-12 (M29m): eight playtest reports in a row, none of which any build, soak or checker had caught. Tinted glass keeps its own per-texel alpha, hostiles spawn by day and burn for it, lava falls as a column, the hotbar and inventory survive a restart, an archer only shoots when it means it, breaking a block **cracks the block itself** and the HUD progress bar is gone — and respawning no longer buries you, because the player now asks whether the ground has loaded before it falls through it.
- **Build:** `. .\tools\dev-env.ps1` then `cmake --build build\release`, run with `.\run.ps1 release`. PowerShell 5.1, chain with `;` and never `&&`.
- **The bar:** both presets clean at `/W4` with zero warnings, and `tools\soak.ps1 -Seconds 45` with zero validation errors and an empty stderr. **That bar proves it does not crash and almost nothing else** — see §7.
- **Never commit to Git. The user is the playtester. Textures are Mojang's on purpose. One agent at a time.** Those catch most new sessions out; §1 and §5 are the long versions.

## 1. The five rules that will otherwise cost the user time

They have paid for each of these once already. Do not make them pay twice.

1. **Never run `git commit` or `git push` unless explicitly asked.** Write files, leave them uncommitted. Direct correction: *"undo those commits. who told you to commit."*
2. **Bedrock Edition is the reference, not Java.** Where they differ, Bedrock wins. `RESEARCH.md` marks Java values `[JE]`.
3. **The user is the playtester, and a good one.** Anything needing aim, a held button, or a judgement about how something *feels* goes to them. They have said "I'm a tool" three times, the last in capitals. **Two failed screenshot-harness attempts is the signal to stop** — restore `settings.cfg` and `saves/*/player.dat`, hand over the build, and say what to look at.
4. **When the user names a milestone, build it.** If it is too big, split it *yourself* and ship the first slice. Handing back a recommendation instead of work is the one thing that has genuinely angered them. Bugs are expected and forgiven; not starting is not.
5. **Launch subagents with `model: "Claude Opus 5 (copilot)"`.** Omitting the parameter silently gets a small model and the work comes back thin. **Subagents only — do not run two agents side by side.** That was tried on 2026-08-11 and removed the same day; §2 says why.

## 3. Where the project actually is

**Milestones 1–29 are done, plus M29b through M29m. `INTERFACE.md` slices 1–5 and 7 are built; 6, 8 and 9 are not.**

> ✅ **The catalogue passed 1300 on 2026-08-11.** The user asked for "at least 300" more blocks and items in one run and got **+313**: the redstone kit (M29h), the whole effect-potion-brewing system (M29i, 124 entries), signs and banners (M29j, 38), and thrown potions plus the collectibles (M29k, 110 — pottery sherds, goat horns, music discs and firework stars). **1343 catalogue entries against 1152 recipes.**

> ⚠ **There is a redstone kit and none of it carries a signal (2026-08-11).** Forty-one craftable things — dust, the torch on a floor or a wall, a lever, twelve buttons, fourteen pressure plates, a repeater, a comparator, both pistons and their head, an observer, a dispenser, a dropper, a daylight detector, a lightning rod, a tripwire hook and four rails — all placing, breaking, crafting, dropping and drawing correctly, and every one of them **inert**. That is the player's own call: *"don't do redstone logic — that's too complex and it's like a week worth of work on its own minimum."* **Do not start the engine unprompted.** The Bedrock rules for it are researched and written into `TIMELINE.md` → M29h.

> ✅ **Block geometry is now measured rather than trusted, and no fault is open (2026-08-11).** `tools/check-models.ps1` compares every block against the reference's own `models/block/*.json`: **1792 checked, 0 disagreeing**, four divergences named as deliberate. It exists because the bed took four rounds of playtesting and every one of them was a rectangle guessed out of a picture instead of read from the model that states it. The same round found that **every dropped block was a spinning cube** — a dropped bell was a gold brick — and made it a miniature of the block instead. top, then the head's end face, then two missing legs — and every one of them was the same mistake: rectangles guessed out of the images instead of read from the reference's own `template_bed_head.json`, which names every face of every box. **When a block is more than a cube, open its JSON first.**

**There are villages, as of M29d.** They stand on a 448-block grid with 160 blocks of separation, one about every 1450 blocks, in five types — plains, desert, savanna, taiga and snowy — chosen by **one biome sample at the town square**. `VillageType` is a column on the biome table, which is the reference's own design: a biome without one never holds a village. Eleven building shapes over five material palettes make fifty-five buildings: three small houses, a medium, a large with a real upper storey and a ladder, a workshop with an open counter onto the street, a library lined with shelves, a temple, a farm with a water channel and four crops, an animal pen, and the town centre — a well under a roof, a bell over it, and four market stalls. Every building rolls its own roof pitch, plinth, window pattern, chimney and bed colour, which is what makes them varied without making them unrelated. **Houses are rigid and roads follow the ground per column**, which is the single distinction that decides whether a hillside village reads as deliberate or broken; the hole under a house is poured with a circular platform and whatever the hill left inside it is carved out.

**The villagers who live there claim their own trades.** A village generates nobody employed — five per cent babies, one adult in ten a nitwit, the rest unemployed — and every armourer you ever meet claimed a blast furnace on its first morning. Claiming is sixteen blocks out and four up, every three to five seconds, **and a villager with no bed will not take a job**. Four new behaviour rows carry the day: they work the morning, gather at the bell through the afternoon, go home at dusk and sleep. Fourteen trades wear fourteen outfits. And **an iron golem comes with the village**, or you can build one out of four iron blocks and a carved pumpkin — a golem you built never turns on you, which in Bedrock is structural rather than a timer.

The game is genuinely playable. An endless seeded world streams in; you walk, sprint, sneak, jump, fly and swim; you break blocks on a timer that depends on block and tool, and place them back. There is a 36-slot inventory with full click/drag/shift-click behaviour, a crafting table, a working furnace, a smoker, a smithing table, a 27-slot chest that joins into a 54-slot double when two stand side by side, twenty-five tools that wear out, torches, and saves that survive a restart.

Underneath: generation and meshing run on worker threads, geometry is greedily merged and frustum culled, and the world has sky light, block light, smooth lighting and ambient occlusion under a placeholder sun.

**There are status effects now, and a brewing stand that makes them.** `world/Effects.hpp` carries twenty-six effects on Bedrock's own numbering, eight active at once, with the reference's overwrite-or-discard rule and a published formula per thing an effect changes — speed, mining, melee, regeneration, poison, wither, absorption, jumping and falling. Forty-one brews exist in four forms each: drunk, thrown as a splash, thrown as a **lingering** cloud that keeps working for thirty seconds, or tipped onto an arrow. Brewing is instant and has no fuel, which is named as a divergence rather than owed.

**Two thousand eight hundred and seventy-one block ids and 1343 catalogue entries**, against 1152 recipes. Seventy-three blocks were hand-written rows; the rest arrived in **seven table-driven runs** — `kExtraBlocks`, indexed by `id - kFirstExtraBlock`, carrying name and texture layers so a new block is one row rather than eight `case` labels scattered across as many switches — and in **five cut-shape runs** whose 640 members carry no art at all, only a parent block. Deepslate and its cobbled form, the polished and brick stone families, sandstone, prismarine, sea lantern, coarse dirt, more flowers, kelp and seagrass. Plus **nine ores** over a deepslate floor on bedrock, glass, and the stone family. **Eleven foods** — apple, and five raw/cooked pairs — which smelt through the same furnace chain as ore and drop from the animals that carry them. **Thirteen resource items** smelt into a metal chain. Ore bands and drop counts are the wiki's, mapped onto our shorter world, and each ore now demands the reference's own tier. **Five tool tiers** — wood, stone, iron, diamond and **Emberite**, our name for the reference's dark alloy, which is smelted from ancient debris and upgraded onto a diamond tool at a **smithing table** rather than crafted — and a **bow**.

**Containers are one code path with several front ends, and that is the cheapest thing in the codebase.** `isChest` is the whole of what a barrel, a trapped chest, an ender chest and seventeen **stowboxes** (our name for the shulker box, since *Shulker* is Mojang's coinage) cost: one screen, one block entity, one spill on break. Two exceptions are carved out deliberately. The **ender chest** resolves to twenty-seven slots the *player* owns, so every one in the world is the same window — checked before the block map is consulted at all. The **stowbox** is the one container whose contents do **not** fall out when it is broken: they move onto the item and ride in the stack's `damage`, which is the one per-stack number `player.dat`, the chest file and a dropped entity already carry, so contents that travel with an item needed no new field and no format bump anywhere. A `static_assert` holds it to a stack of one, because two merging would silently pick one set of contents and lose the other. The **hopper** is the same struct again with five of its slots used and a screen to match, moving one item every eight ticks — pushing out of its spout, then pulling from whatever is above it.

**Doors, trapdoors and beds went in on 2026-08-10, and they are what a village is built out of.** Twelve door families of **thirty-two states each** — four facings times a hinge side times open times which half — packed into the offset so every fact about a door is a bit or two of it. Placing one sets both halves and puts the hinge on whichever side has something solid; the reference stores the hinge rather than deriving it, because the same neighbourhood can carry either hand depending on what stood there when it was hung. Right-clicking swings both halves together, and breaking either takes the other while dropping exactly one door. Twelve trapdoor families at sixteen states each, hung in the top or bottom half by where you were looking. And sixteen beds, two blocks apiece, that **set your respawn point and skip the night**. `kDoorFamilies`, `kTrapdoorFamilies` and `kWoods` are declared in the *same order* on purpose — the recipe loop indexes straight across them, so a different order there would quietly give a cherry door a mangrove recipe.

> **Named divergence: an iron door opens by hand.** The reference answers only to a signal, and there is no redstone here — a door nobody could open would be worse than the divergence.

**There is a farm, as of 2026-08-10.** A hoe tills dirt, grass and a trodden path into farmland; a shovel makes the path. Wheat, carrots, potatoes and beetroot each keep their age **in the block id** the way water keeps its level, and grow on the reference's own arithmetic — `1 / (floor(25 / points) + 1)`, where the points come from the **three-by-three patch of farmland under and around the plant**, not from the plant. Melon and pumpkin stems ripen and then put a fruit on an adjacent cell, checking the block *beneath* the candidate rather than the candidate itself, and attach to it until it is taken. Farmland dries out and reverts to dirt only when **nothing is planted on it**, so dry farming is legitimate rather than doomed. Bone meal is a random tick you asked for — it runs the same rule the sampler does — and beetroot takes a single stage three times in four, which is why it is poor value on it. Falling on a field wrecks it with probability `fallDistance − 0.5`, harvesting whatever was growing. A composter takes twenty-odd plant materials at the reference's own five chance bands and yields bone meal at level eight. Shears carve a pumpkin, and a carved pumpkin plus a torch is a lantern. `world/Farming.hpp` owns every number.

**Two hundred and fifteen entries were added in that same batch.** Twenty bark blocks and their stripped forms (no new art at all — they point at log sides already staged), mushroom blocks, the full coral family alive and dead as blocks, plants and fans, waxed copper, copper grates, copper bulbs that dim as they oxidise (15/12/8/4), seventeen candles, the two-block flowers, the sculk family, amethyst buds, dripleaves, cave vines, chorus plants, and the village workstations. Plus **seventy-four items**: twenty-four pieces of armour carrying Bedrock's real defence and toughness values, a turtle shell, a shield, fifteen records, eighteen pieces of equipment, four bowls of stew, and six buckets with a fish in them. **Emberite armour is a smithing upgrade**, like its tools.

> **Deliberately simplified, and worth knowing before you file a bug:** the **loom, brewing stand and anvil** are placeable but inert — the first two need banners and potions, which do not exist, and adding either system for one block would be a bigger job than every workstation already built. Chainmail has no recipe, exactly as it has none in the reference (it drops from the undead instead). Everything else on that list has since been done properly: the **lectern holds a book**, the **stonecutter cuts stairs, slabs and walls** from one block, the **bell rings**, the **cauldron fills and empties** with a bucket or a bottle, the **grindstone repairs**, the **barrel, trapped chest, ender chest and seventeen stowboxes are real containers**, the **hopper moves items**, the **blast furnace smelts** at double speed, **farmland is genuinely 15/16**, and **candles stack one to four with the light following the count**.

**Seven of those workstations stopped being cubes at M29e.** The bell, cauldron, composter, grindstone, stonecutter, brewing stand and the torch are `BlockShape::Model` now, built box for box from the reference's own `models/block/*.json`. Before that they were full opaque cubes, which meant each one culled its neighbours' faces and you could see through the world for a couple of blocks around a cauldron.

**Fifty-seven creature species** share the world — twenty-three animals, two passive folk (a **villager** and a **wandering trader**), and sixteen hostiles: the **Bramble** (our creeper analogue), **slimes** in three sizes that split when killed, the **spider** and **cave spider**, which climb walls and only hunt in the dark, the **zombie**, **skeleton**, **Blackbone**, **stray**, **bogged**, **zombie villager** and **witch**, the bipeds, the **husk**, the **silverfish**, the **Princepin**, the only hostile that spawns in daylight, and the **drowned**, which walks the seabed. They spawn by biome and light, wander, flee, jump ledges, and two are neutral (wolf and polar bear). A share of every natural group is young, and the population survives a restart.

**The sea is inhabited, as of M20i.** Nine aquatic species and a whole second movement model: **cod**, **salmon**, **pufferfish**, **tropical fish**, **squid**, **glow squid**, **turtle**, **dolphin** and **axolotl**. A swimmer has no gravity and steers in three dimensions; a **pufferfish** inflates through three genuinely different models when you get within 2.5 m; a **squid** jets — its tentacles flare slowly and snap shut, and *the snap is what pushes it*, so it must turn about before it can go the other way; a **glow squid** lights itself; a **turtle** hatches on beach sand and swims only once it reaches the water. Nothing spawns in a puddle: every aquatic needs an ocean biome and three blocks of water depth.

**Aggression is the reference's, as of M20f.** A hostile has to *see* you to notice you — that predicate was missing entirely, which is why everything used to track you through rock. It scans twice a second rather than every frame, forgets a target it has lost sight of on the species' own timer (three seconds for most, **seventeen for a zombie**), notices you at one range and gives up at another (a zombie spots you at **35 m** and gives up at 25), holds a grudge for its own length (a wolf 25 seconds, a polar bear 500), and has to be *facing* you within 90° to land a blow that reaches as far as its own body is wide. Striking one no longer summons the undead: only some species call for help, and the reference's zombies and skeletons are not among them.

**They are properly animated.** Limbs hang from a joint and **rotate** about it rather than sliding, on an eased amplitude that spins up and winds down; heads turn **about the neck** and tip up and down to watch you; bipeds sway their arms when idle. **Stepping up a block eases the drawn body after the box** — for creatures and, since 2026-08-05, for the player's camera too, so a staircase no longer reads as a series of teleports.

**And as of M20j they fight properly.** A hostile closes on you, **stops when it arrives** and swings — it used to walk straight through, overshoot and orbit you, landing a blow on every pass, because a chase had no arrival condition at all. A blow swings the arms on the reference's own curves, and the two rigs run in opposite senses: a zombie starts with its arms out and **chops down**, an armed biped starts with them hanging and **swings up**. Which mobs swing is a **species** fact rather than a rig one — the skeleton family are **archers** and deliberately do not, while the Blackbone does, because it carries a sword. A **slime rebounds off you** like a wall and comes again, which is better than the reference here: Bedrock separates the two bodies with entity pushing, which we have no equivalent of.

**The spider was rebuilt at M20j** from `geometry.spider.v1.8` and `animation.spider.walk`. Its body used to sit low with eight level bars either side of it; the reference droops each leg 45° about its own forward axis from a joint level with the body, and **that droop is the entire reason a spider stands off the ground**. The walk is the reference's exactly — a quarter turn of phase per pair, a sweep at twice the rate of the lift, absolute values on both — and what keeps adjacent leg tips from colliding is the *lift*, not the sweep.

**The Bramble detonates.** A real blast: the reference's 1352-ray block algorithm, an exposure test so cover protects, and damage on the player *and* the population. It stops dead to swell within 2.5 m, needs line of sight for the whole countdown, gives up past 6 m, runs from cats, and a hard landing shortens its fuse. **Charged ones** carry the reference's blue energy shell and twice the power.

**The inventory has a second card.** Five tabs — Construction, Equipment, Items, Nature, Search — over every item in the game, clickable in creative to take a stack, with the empty space around the entries acting as a bin. It **scrolls**, and the row the card cuts through is clipped by a real scissor rectangle rather than left blank. **Fifty-six spawn eggs** are reached from there rather than the hotbar; right-click to place that creature. A **bucket** made from three iron ingots picks water up and puts it back down.

**A furnace faces the way you placed it**, with the mouth on one side and `furnace_side` on the other three. That needed side faces to know which way they point, which nothing in the mesher used to expose — `FaceDirection` now does, and **the crafting table uses it too**: the tooled face on its two Z sides, the plainer one on its X sides, fixed rather than a placement state. **An item icon asks for a direction as well**, because it draws two side faces at once and handing both the same one put a furnace's mouth on the right-hand face of every icon in the inventory.

**Reach is 5 m for blocks and 3 m for entities** (5 in creative), which are Bedrock's mouse values. It was 12 m for a long time — that is Bedrock's *touch creative* number and was simply the wrong row of the table.

**World generation was rebuilt on the reference's own architecture at M20p, then corrected twice by playtesting at M20q and M20r (2026-08-07).** A biome no longer decides how tall the land is — terrain and biome are both outputs of the same **five** climate fields (temperature, humidity, continentalness, erosion, weirdness), which is the change the reference itself made in its 1.18 rewrite. Splines turn those into a target height, a **`factor`** saying how hard that target is enforced, and a jaggedness; the height is then computed **directly per column**, exactly, with no interpolation lattice. **Twenty-seven biomes** each claim a *box* in that space rather than a centre with a falloff, and a `BiomeTag` bitmask is how everything else asks questions — so the fifty creature spawn rules never had to name a biome. **Rivers fall out of the ridge field's zero contour** and are not a system. Three cave systems, ores as **placed veins with a stated maximum size**, and surface rules as a real top-down sequence.

**Four rules there are guarantees rather than tunings, and every one came from a playtest bug.** Terrain is **single-valued**, so floating land is impossible by construction — but note that this *reshapes* a would-be island into a sheer pillar rather than preventing one, which is why `factor` must stay high (4.6–6.2) everywhere except a narrow peak window. A biome names what it *scatters* and everything else falls through to its ordinary top block, so `else stone` — which produced rings of bare stone — cannot be written. `steep` puts bare rock on steep faces, which is the difference between a peak and a white blob. And **a bed material is gated on the waterline, never on the biome**: the reference does not name `river` in its surface rules at all, so a dry river is grass rather than a ribbon of gravel across a field. `SYSTEM_MEMORY.md` → "World Generation" has the detail and `RESEARCH.md` §15 the research.

**Four more systems landed on 2026-08-07, all from playtest reports.** **Waterlogging** — one bit per cell beside the block array, not a second block id — so kelp and seagrass stop punching plant-shaped holes in the ocean; `canWaterlog` is a *shape* test and is **Cross only**, because a block that fills its cell has to cut the water supply off rather than run around it. **Falling blocks**: sand and gravel detach and become a real entity under half the player's gravity, testing every cell they pass through so a long drop cannot tunnel a ledge. **Ore veins were rewritten as placed features** — the reference's `OreFeature` spindle of overlapping spheres, so a vein's maximum size is *stated* rather than an accident of where a noise field happened to sit high, which is what produced a "humongous" coal seam. And **fog became radial** rather than cylindrical (it was measuring `gl_Position.w`, which is depth along the view axis, so the world curved), which then paid for itself: culling anything beyond the fog took draws from 308 to 235 and triangles from 1.30 M to 1.04 M.

**A large bug sweep on 2026-08-08 found ten real faults in code that had passed "both presets clean" many times.** The two worst were invisible: **the axe, shovel, sword and hoe could not be crafted at any tier** (a helper padded their patterns to 3×3 while the matcher compares against the bounding box, so only the pickaxe — the one shape filling all three columns — ever matched), and **about two hundred of the appended blocks dropped nothing when broken by hand**, because the second block run defaulted every one of them to needing a wood-tier tool. Also fixed: water and lava drew a surface only against literal air, so a lily pad, torch, fence or pane of glass standing beside them **erased the surface there** — reported as "holes in the water"; a roof left the whole column under it at full sky light; two falling blocks in one shaft crushed each other; the cactus rendered as an opaque cube over see-through art; the three slimes and three magma cubes all shared one name, so six spawn eggs were indistinguishable; and the salmon dropped cod. The lily pad also stopped being a plant *standing in* a cell and became `BlockShape::Flat`, resting **on** the water — `restsOnWater` is the one block whose support is not solid. The method is worth reusing and is recorded in `LESSONS.md`: a temporary startup pass that walks every block, item, recipe and species and **cross-checks the tables against the loaded textures**, plus scripted world scenarios, a slot-operation fuzz, and a "the world must be identical six seconds later" snapshot.

**Then the recipe table was checked against the catalogue, and went from 60 to 340.** *"make sure crafteable items are crafteable"* — and most of them were not. **Only oak wood did anything**: spruce and birch had a wrong-rate plank recipe and the other eight woods had none, so eight of the eleven forests were scenery. **Stairs and slabs had no recipe at all.** The whole colour chain was missing — twelve flowers now give their dyes, which feed wool, terracotta and concrete powder, sixty-four blocks that had no source between them. Most of the table is **generated in loops** (eleven woods × eleven shapes, sixteen colours × three families), and every one of the 340 is checked to make itself with no two claiming the same pattern. What is left unobtainable is thirty-two entries waiting on farming, bee harvesting or the nether — a system each, not a recipe.

**M20w then took the block count from 395 to 1094 and added the bow.** *"make sure the scale is enormous"*. There was exactly **one** stair family in the game, one slab and one fence; the reference has them for about fifty materials, and that was the largest hole in what you could build. `ShapedFamily` fixed it in one stroke: a row carries a **parent block**, and `shapedParent` forwards the texture, the tool, the hardness, the blast resistance and whether it burns — so **640 blocks arrived with no new art and no new row in any of those tables**. 52 stair families, 55 slabs, 25 walls, 12 fences, 11 gates that swing open, plus 16 stained glass, 17 panes, iron bars, 16 carpets, five light sources and a **ladder you climb**. 592 recipes now, all of them checked to make themselves.

**And projectiles are real.** The bow draws on the reference's **quadratic** curve, its arrows fly on a **fixed twenty-hertz tick** because every number the reference publishes is per tick, and the physics was verified against the closed form to one part in a million. Damage comes from the speed the arrow is doing *now*, not from how fast it left — so a long shot lands softer and one through water barely lands at all. Blocks are swept before entities and the sweep covers the whole segment, so nothing tunnels at sixty blocks a second. **The skeleton family finally have something to shoot**: `shootsArrows` is the other half of the split that already recorded them as archers who deliberately do not mime a sword swing. `RESEARCH.md` §17 has the numbers.

**M20x added the jungle.** Three biomes — jungle, sparse jungle and bamboo jungle — and the biome table needed a **new climate axis** to hold them: the reference splits them on the *sign* of weirdness, and `ridges` folds that sign away. Trees come in the reference's own mix (45% bushes, 15% two-by-two giants, a fancy oak, and the small jungle tree), and **vines are sixteen ids** — one per combination of the four sides they cling to, which is Bedrock's own count. `trunk_vine` sheaths every log at 75% a side and `leave_vine` hangs curtains four blocks down off the canopy; **cocoa** is four facings times three ages on the lowest logs of a small tree, and its beans are the reference's brown dye. Only **shears** collect a vine, which needed a tool *kind* rather than a tier. Measured across forty jungle chunks: 9,995 vines, 32 pods.

**M20y made the shapes tell the truth**, and every item on its list came from someone looking at the game rather than at the code. Four of them had been wrong since the feature was written and had simply never had an asymmetric texture, a transparent icon or a lone pane put in front of them: the **+X and −Z faces of every shaped block were mirrored** (which is why lit TNT read backwards while ordinary TNT did not), a **connecting shape's collision assumed every arm** (so a lone pane of glass was an invisible cross), **a face was culled when only its middle was covered** (so you could see through the top of every lantern), and **a blended fragment writing depth** let the stack on your cursor punch a hole through the catalogue behind it. Models now carry a texture rectangle **per face**, which is what a lantern and an end rod actually need, and the **void pearl is a real arcing throw** that puts you where it stopped or nowhere at all. It also gave the catalogue **a search field**, because 640 new cut shapes had buried everything else — TNT is at row 16 of 58 in a card seven rows tall.

**M20z was the same again, for text and motion.** The font is now **Mojang's own `ascii.png`**, proportional, with every glyph's width **measured off whichever atlas loaded** rather than written down — and our placeholder regenerated in their exact layout so either drops into the other's place. Three of the round's bugs were one bug: something drawn once and never drawn again. Glyph quads overlapped and the depth test ate two columns off every letter after the first; the hotbar was built once when the bow started drawing and not again until the arrow left; and projectiles were drawn *on* their twenty-hertz tick, so a 120 fps screen showed each position six frames running. **The physics tick did not move** — the drawing did, interpolating between ticks, which is the rule to reach for whenever a fixed step looks choppy.

**M21 made the world able to kill you (2026-08-08).** Twenty hearts, twenty hunger, and a hidden saturation buffer above the bar. Damage follows the reference's **overwrite rule** rather than a plain cooldown — a bigger blow inside the half-second window still lands, for the difference — which is the whole reason a creeper is dangerous rather than absorbed by whatever hit you a moment earlier. Hunger drains by **exhaustion**, not by time, so standing still costs nothing; below 6 you cannot sprint, at 18 you regenerate, and at 0 you starve to half a heart. Fall damage, drowning, suffocation, fire, lava, burning after you leave it, cactus and the void. Eating is **held for 1.6 seconds**, not clicked. Dying drops your inventory and respawns you. `world/Survival.hpp` owns every number; `hud/StatusBars.hpp` draws the three bars.

**M22 gave it sound (2026-08-08).** **miniaudio** opens the device, `stb_vorbis` decodes, and `engine::AudioEngine` mixes 48 voices at 48 kHz with distance rolloff and a shallow pan — knowing nothing about blocks or creatures. `game::Sounds` owns the mapping: **57 events and 34 creature voice families**, 497 recordings, up to eight per event picked at random and pitched slightly differently every time. Blocks resolve to one of **ten materials by family test**, so eleven hundred of them are covered by a dozen questions and six hundred stairs and slabs come free through `shapedParent`. Creatures resolve to a voice **family, not a species**, and a baby is pitched up from the adult's own recording. Footsteps, digging, hurt, the two fall sounds, splashes, cave ambience, eating, the bow pitched by its draw, arrows, explosions, fuses, buckets, chest lids, gates, pickups, and every creature's idle, hurt and death cry.

### What is in flight right now

- **Mobs fight at range properly as of 2026-08-11 (M29l), and it is the one thing still needing your eye.** No creature had ever rendered a **held item** of any kind; the mechanism turned out to be free, because a creature quad carrying a *non-negative* texture layer already reaches the block-and-item pictures where the skin sheet is a negative one. So a bow goes through `appendSpriteModel`, the same owner a dropped item already uses. Archers carry one in the **right** hand, raise it when they see you and shoot **from the hand** rather than the chest; witches **throw splash potions** instead of walking into you. Three reference numbers were corrected on the way: the interval is **3 s, not 1** (bogged 3.5), everything in `minecraft:behavior.ranged_attack` is in **seconds**, and **there is no bow wind-up in Bedrock at all** — the pose is gated on "do I have a target" and the interval is a reload behind an already-drawn bow. **Not verified by eye:** stand off a skeleton at night and check the bow is in the hand and the arrow leaves it, and let a witch see you.
- **The bed is finished as of 2026-08-10, after four rounds of playtesting.** Its top is a single face — pillow rows 0–7, the pillow's shadow row 8, blanket rows 9–15 — sampled whole through `lidTurns`, so the pillow is half the head block and blanket covers the rest. The head's outward end has its own shared texture, `bed_head_north.png`, because the long-side image is half blanket and painted the headboard red down one half. And the head's legs read u 13–16 of the side net rather than the foot's u 0–3, or they sample empty texture and the bed stands on two. **One new texture layer, appended at the very end.**
- **Fifty-three of the fifty-seven creature skins are Mojang placeholders**, as are all 57 spawn egg sprites, the five catalogue tabs and every block and item texture. This is **deliberate and sanctioned** — see §5. Do not "fix" it.
- **Water physics were rebuilt on 2026-08-05** and the old fudge is gone. Three halves, recorded as **M20h**, with `world/Fluid.hpp` and `SYSTEM_MEMORY.md` → "Water" now the owners — `RESEARCH.md` §9.1 was retired to a pointer once the work shipped. **Entities:** water no longer weakens gravity, it replaces the model with the reference's multiplicative drag, so sinking, swimming, sprint-swimming, the plunge after a dive and being carried by a current are all one expression. Breath and drowning exist, dropped items float, and creatures follow the reference's navigation flags — a cow bobs, a zombie walks the seabed, a Princepin drowns. **The block:** falling water is its own block and is full, a cell that can drop never runs sideways (so a waterfall is a column, not a cone), and a weight search sends a stream at the nearest hole within four blocks. Seven blocks of spread sideways, unlimited downward, paced at the reference's five ticks a block. Plants are washed away and dropped rather than damming the flow. The surface plays its thirty-two frame animation, redirected in the fragment shader so no chunk is re-meshed for it. **The look:** real distance fog, not a tint — and **its colour is measured off screenshots, not taken from Bedrock's fog JSON.** `SYSTEM_MEMORY.md` has a do-not-revert box; read it before changing that constant, because the obvious correction is wrong and has been made twice. `world/Fluid.hpp` owns every water constant. **Not done and deliberate:** the directional `water_flow` texture (32×32 against our 16×16 array, and it needs per-cell UV rotation), lava, the swimming *pose*, and the reference's eyes-adjusting fog ramp (built, then removed — it restarts on every dip). **The bubble bar exists** — it arrived beside the heart bar as planned, ten bubbles of thirty ticks each, `static_assert`ed against the air clock so the two cannot drift.
- **Mobs no longer spawn inside blocks**, and the loading screen no longer finishes early. Both were 2026-08-05 and both were the same shape of bug: a value derived somewhere other than the table that owns it. A spawn candidate now clears its real body box through the shared collision helpers instead of scanning whole cells, anything that ends up buried climbs out, and the loading bar streams around the player's *saved* position rather than the generator's spawn point — the first log line went from `pending 372` to `pending 0`.
- **M20b's archetypes are complete.** The **flying** archetype landed with the bee: `flies` is the airborne mirror of `swims` — no gravity, a heading in three dimensions, no pathfinder — plus a 2–6 block height band, a dive angle while chasing, and no knockback, because a flier's own locomotion owns every axis of its velocity. The **water** archetype landed at M20i, the melee behaviour at M20j, **pathfinding at M20k** — creatures now search a real route with A\* and fall back to the old steering fan when they have none, so a wall is something to walk around rather than press against — and **the death fall at M20m**: a killed creature keeps its damage tint, tips a quarter turn onto its side and lies there before it goes, driven off the shared rig so all fifty-seven species get it with no per-species table. `TIMELINE.md` has the list.
- **`INTERFACE.md` slice 6 is next** on the interface side. Slice 4 landed the catalogue's scrolling; **slice 5 landed the craftable colouring** — **four** cell backgrounds, not the six vanilla's UI data lists, read from the recipe table and answered against the grid the open screen has. Three of vanilla's six are expandable groups (slice 9) and the fourth was a *selected* state the user rejected twice: hovering may brighten a cell, but nothing stays lit.
- **Storage and the three utility blocks landed at M20o.** A **smoker** (a furnace that runs at double speed and cost no new screen, because `isFurnace` answers for both families), a **smithing table** (which is where the Emberite upgrade moved to), and a **chest** — 27 slots, or 54 when two stand side by side sharing a facing. The pairing is **derived from position every time, never stored**, so it needs no save data and the two halves cannot disagree.
- **Do not re-tune any water constant by eye — run `tools/simulate-swim.ps1`.** It replays the vertical motion and reads every constant out of the headers, so it cannot drift from the code. Water was corrected twice after M20h and treading took three attempts; `SYSTEM_MEMORY.md` → "Water" explains what each knob does and `LESSONS.md` has the three failed attempts.
- **Nothing damages the player yet.** ~~Blasts and blows apply knockback only, because player health is M21.~~ **Fixed at M21** — blasts and blows now apply their damage, and creative immunity arrives through `PlayerInput::invulnerable` rather than by the survival code knowing what mode the game is in.
- **The next milestone is M30, hardware ray tracing** — the first of the frontier work, and optional. M23 through M29 are all done, **M29b closed the performance and memory work that sat behind them**, and none of them owes anything any more (2026-08-10). What is left after M30 is M31 advanced simulation, M32 global illumination, M33 tooling, and the two that actually finish the game: **M34 settings and accessibility** and **M35 packaging**.

> **The sun and moon's orientation is settled as of 2026-08-09, after four failed attempts.** The player wanted a square that is upright when you face it at sunrise, overhead or sunset, and stands on a corner when you face one of the four diagonals. **The blocker was never the quad — it was the arc**, which had been tilted 15.6° out of the east-overhead-west plane so the sun would miss the zenith and keep lighting walls at noon. Any square referenced to the world rolls by however far the arc misses the camera's own vertical plane, which reached 36° by mid-morning. The arc now passes through the zenith and the quad is spanned by the arc's axis and its tangent; measured 0.000° off square in every case the player named. `SYSTEM_MEMORY.md` → "Sun, moon and sky" has the reasoning and the one accepted cost.
>
> Three related things in the same area are also fixed and verified: the faint square halo around both bodies (the alpha derived from their additive art never reached zero), them appearing to sink into nearby ground (they now sit just inside the far plane), and them dissolving into distance fog as they set (`kDrawFlagSky`).

**M23 restructured the renderer (2026-08-09).** Physically based materials, a G-buffer, HDR and tone mapping, in six slices — `m23planning.md` has the plan and `TIMELINE.md` the result. A frame is now **eight passes**: shadow, geometry, deferred lighting, **scene copy**, forward, bloom, tone map, UI. **ACES is the default tone curve**, chosen by the player after comparing all four on screen; `F10` cycles them and the F5 overlay names the one you are on. Roughness, metallic and emissive live in one packed word **per texture layer**, so six hundred cut shapes inherit their parent's answer for nothing. `F12` cycles ten surface debug views — that is how a deferred renderer is read.

**M24 gave the world real shadows (2026-08-09).** Cascaded shadow maps: the world rendered from the light's own point of view into two to four slices of the distance ahead of you, sharp underfoot and coarse far off. `G` cycles quality, `shadows` in `settings.cfg` is the same number, and off is a real setting. **One directional light, not two** — whichever of the sun and moon is above the horizon owns it, so moonlight casts shadows through the same cascades and the night has a lit side. The moon runs the reference's eight phases, one per day. Two things in there look like mistakes and are not: **the shadow pass culls nothing** (a voxel mesh is a hollow shell, so front-face culling — the usual acne cure — would leave flat ground casting nothing at all), and **each cascade is fitted to a sphere and snapped to whole texels** (anything else makes every shadow edge crawl as you turn). Costs 2.24 ms of GPU against an 8.3 ms budget at medium.

**M25 gave the sky a shape (2026-08-09).** Blocky raymarched clouds whose coverage is quantised to the reference's own 12-block grid and thresholded hard, so a cloud is built from square pieces rather than smooth blobs — the player rejected smooth ones explicitly. The deck sits at y 140, cloud shadows fall on the ground, and the sky is a gradient written by the lighting pass wherever nothing was drawn, with its horizon **exactly** the fog colour so the join is invisible. `C` cycles cloud quality. Still owed: real atmospheric scattering and altitude effects.

**M26 made water reflect (2026-08-09).** A copy of the lit world is taken between the lighting pass and the forward pass, and water marches a ray through it — so it reflects the bank and the trees, not just the sky. **Alpha in the scene image is a distance, not an opacity**, which is what lets one copy serve as both the colour to reflect and the depth to measure thickness against; that thickness drives Beer's law, so a pond is clear at its edge and solid in the middle. **Reflections are pixelated on purpose** — the player asked for it, and everything is computed from a position snapped to the block texture's own grid. Fresnel is the physical fifth power: 2% looking straight down, nearly a mirror along the surface, and judging it from a steep angle will make it look broken when it is not. Shadows also darken the ambient sky now (`shadow_darkness`, default 0.55), because cutting the sun alone left them reading as pale patches.

**M27 brought weather (2026-08-09).** Rain, snow, thunderstorms and lightning. **Two independent flags with their own countdowns, not a three-way state** — a storm is rain and thunder overlapping, which is why they are rare. Rain and snow are **one vertical quad per world column**, and that choice answers the roof and cave question for free: the quad starts at the top of whatever blocks that column, so there is no shelter test anywhere. The streaks are procedural rather than a texture so they land on the block grid. Lightning is midpoint displacement drawn white and emissive, and its flash is **two to four return strokes** because a single fade reads as a camera going off. `V` forces rain / storm / clear; **`start_weather` in `settings.cfg` is the reliable way to see one**, because the screenshot harness's keypresses are not.

**M28 added particles and a wind (2026-08-09).** Breaking a block throws off chips of its own texture, rain makes flecks where it lands, a hard fall kicks up a puff. **Simulated on the CPU and drawn through the existing lit cutout path** — no new pipeline, no compute, no instancing; "GPU-driven" was a vision-document phrase and three thousand quads do not need it. They **shrink as they die rather than fading**, because the cutout path throws a fragment away below half alpha and a ramp would blink them out whole. Grass and leaves now bend with the same wind vector that drifts the clouds and slants the rain — always *along* the wind, never oscillating through zero, because grass bends and does not wag. `particles` and `foliage_sway` in `settings.cfg`.

**M29 finished the image (2026-08-09).** Contact shadows off the depth buffer the lighting pass already reads — no extra pass, eight taps, 0.2 ms — catching what the mesher's baked occlusion cannot: a creature's feet, a dropped item, two surfaces meeting far from any vertex. And an anti-aliaser that runs **after** the tone curve (before it, HDR ratios swamp the blend) and is **off by default**, because everything here is a hard-edged square and softening diagonals softens every texel boundary too. Motion blur and depth of field were declined on purpose.

**Every loose end M25–M29 left behind was closed on 2026-08-10.** The sky is now real single scattering — Rayleigh in the reference's own wavelength proportions, Mie haze, both phase functions, an air-mass term — applied as a **ratio against its own horizon value**, so the join with fogged terrain stays exact while everything above it is physical; plus an exaggerated altitude term and a night that is genuinely dark, because the player reported the old blue one as reading like daytime. **Rain darkens and glosses what it lands on**, splashes on water as well as ground, and **settles as snow**: seven layer depths that cost no art at all, since the eighth is the solid snow cube that already existed. **Ice forms on still water.** **A lightning bolt now does something** — damage, a fire, and a charged Bramble, which is where a charged one was always supposed to come from; the fire is safe only because the same storm now puts fires out. **Torches, fire and furnaces smoke**, eating throws crumbs of the food's own sprite, a blast leaves a smoke ball, and **ground cover comes in patches** rather than an even speckle, with the three snowy biomes no longer barren. **Underwater light shafts** march the same caustic field that draws the net on the seabed. And **`render_scale`** draws the world at a fraction of the window while leaving the interface full size — measured 2.42 ms to 2.11 ms, a small honest return, because this frame is bound by the shadow pass and the triangle count rather than by pixels.

> **Potions were listed as owed and there are none in the game** — no item, no brewing, no effect system. That is a milestone, not a particle.

**M29b made the world cheap to look at (2026-08-10).** The frame was bound by triangles, and a throwaway probe attributing every one of them moved the whole plan: plants were 13.7% of the geometry, but **65% of it sat in the bottom third of the world** — cave walls sealed inside rock that can never be seen from anywhere. So **`detail_distance`** was built as a *rendering* tier. Within it, everything as before. Beyond it, terrain only: plants and vines are not built, a canopy becomes a hollow shell instead of solid leaves, distant water stops being displaced so an ocean can finally merge into big quads, and **any face that receives no light at all is dropped** — which is safe by construction, because light here is a flood fill and an opening big enough to see through is exactly what would have lit it. Creatures, dropped items and projectiles are culled to the same radius.

**They all still exist.** Creatures out there tick, path, spawn, despawn and are saved; plants still break, burn and wash away. Only the triangles are skipped, and they are built again the moment something comes into range. The boundary carries one chunk of hysteresis so pacing across it re-meshes a ring once rather than every step, and the tier is an **input to the mesh job** rather than something a worker looks up — meshing being a pure function of its input volume is what lets it run off the main thread at all. Setting `detail_distance` to the render distance turns it off, which is what makes it something to compare against.

**The measured result, and the row that matters is the last:** render distance 6 goes 428 fps → **481** and 3.03 M triangles → **2.22 M**; render distance 12 goes 282 → **307** and 6.76 M → **5.67 M**; render distance 16 goes 242 → **281** and 8.82 M → **6.71 M**. **Render distance 16 with the tier on costs the same as render distance 12 with it off.** The win was never the frame rate at a fixed distance — it is that you can see half again as far for the same price. `tools/compare-frame.ps1` runs that whole table in one command.

The same round paid off the **sub-allocator owed since M4**: buffers come out of shared 32 MiB blocks, so live GPU allocations went **3100 → 26**. That matters because Vulkan's cap on them has a spec floor of 4096 and render distance 16 had already gone past it — the failure mode being the world silently refusing to appear. And a **temporary verification harness, run and deleted**, found seven real bugs, the worst being **two whole table runs of blocks that no explosion could destroy**. `TIMELINE.md` → M29b has the full list.

**Then the tier was reported as "working but kinda"** — plants appearing a few paces ahead while flying. Measured, the closest chunk drawn at the wrong tier was **zero**, the one underfoot: the mesh queue is a stack and entries arrive in effectively random order, so a tier upgrade landed anywhere. It is drained **nearest-first** now, a dropped re-mesh is recovered rather than stranding a chunk for ever (`detailWanted` vs `detailBuilt`), queueing is O(1), and `gatherVolume` copies **a row at a time into the job's own storage** instead of walking cells and then copying 118 KB. Afterwards only the ring *at* the boundary is ever behind, and it settles to zero when you stop — watch the F5 `tier lag` row. **Choosing the two distances matters more than any of that: 10 against 12 is a two-chunk band that pays the whole re-meshing cost and saves almost nothing.**

**And 552 MB of memory.** Every sound was decoded up to interleaved stereo `float` and kept for the session, which is four times what a mono sixteen-bit clip needs — against 497 recordings and eight music tracks. **1495 MB → 943 MB**, frame unchanged, output bit-identical.

### The shape everything else hangs off (M20c)
Creature AI is **not** a state machine. Eight behaviours sit in a `constexpr` table selected by priority with `Move` / `Look` / `Jump` control flags. Two ideas carry it, and both are worth understanding before adding any behaviour:

1. **Control flags.** Rows claiming *disjoint* flags run at the same time; rows claiming the *same* flag are exclusive and resolved by priority. **A row claiming nothing always runs** — that is not a degenerate case, it is how targeting works.
2. **Target production is split from consumption.** Some rows *write* the target; `MeleeAttack` *reads* it and never asks why it is set. Retaliation, pack anger and hunting-on-sight are three rows that never mention each other.

`canStart` and `canContinue` are deliberately different questions — a hunter gives up further out than it engages, and **a sneaking player is only harder to *notice***, never harder to escape from.

`SYSTEM_MEMORY.md` "How a creature decides what to do" has the row table. `RESEARCH.md` §8.8 step 5 (unify the two spawners) is the only part still open.

## 4. Build and run

```powershell
. .\tools\dev-env.ps1          # once per terminal — the leading dot is required
cmake --build build\release    # or build\debug
.\run.ps1 release              # or debug
```

- **PowerShell 5.1.** Chain with `;`, never `&&`. Never paste multi-line scripts into the terminal — they get mangled.
- **`Start-Process` needs an absolute path** (`"$PWD\build\release\bin\game.exe"`), or it fails with a confusing "cannot find the file".
- **Debug build with zero Vulkan validation errors is the acceptance bar.** Run it before calling anything done.
- **Never benchmark on Debug** — the debug CRT serialises the heap and the numbers are not just noisy, they are non-monotonic. Repeat any timing at least three times and report the minimum.
- **Close the game with `CloseMainWindow()`, never a force-kill** — the save path runs after the window closes.
- **Anything that writes `settings.cfg` or a save must restore it.** A benchmark once left `frame_cap=0` behind and the user reported the limiter broken. Twice.

**Keys worth knowing while testing.** `F1`/`F2` frame cap, `F3`/`F4` field of view, `F5` diagnostics overlay, `F6`/`F7` render distance, **`F8` spawns a Bramble 12 m ahead, `F9` a charged one**. Right-click a spawn egg to place that creature; take one from the inventory's left card.

**`creature_showcase` in `settings.cfg` freezes the spawner** and lines the roster up in front of spawn: `1` is every species in a staggered grid, and **`2` and above is one species alone** in three copies — profile, facing the camera, facing away — where the value is the `CreatureKind` index + 2. It is the wrong tool for anything about *behaviour*, because frozen creatures never act; use `F8` for that. **Restore it to `0` when you are done**, like anything else that writes `settings.cfg`.

**`tools/simulate-swim.ps1` replays the vertical water physics on the CPU** and prints the bob height, the period, how far the eyes ride above the surface and how much of the body is out. It reads every constant out of `Fluid.hpp` and `Player.hpp` rather than copying them, so it cannot drift from the code. Use it instead of playtesting any water tuning — `-PoolDepth 1` checks a one-block puddle, `-Sprint` checks sprint-swimming, and `-TryFloatEye`/`-TryStroke`/`-TryTread` sweep a value without editing the header.

**`worldgen_probe=1` in `settings.cfg` censuses the generated world and exits**, without opening a window. Surface range, share of the world under water, every biome's share **and its top block**, cave volume, per-ore counts, and the number of solid cells above the terrain — which is floating land and must read zero. It is to terrain what `simulate-swim` is to water, and it exists because "both presets build clean with zero validation errors" has never once said anything about whether the world is right: it caught caves being flooded wholesale, humidity clamped so hard that forests nearly vanished, iron outnumbering coal, and peaks too smooth for the steep rule to fire. **Run it after any change to terrain**, and restore the setting to `0` afterwards.

**`tools/check-models.ps1` measures every block against the reference's own `models/block/*.json`** and names any whose size disagrees by more than half a texel. It runs the game once with `block_probe=1`, which dumps `block-shapes.txt` and exits, then compares the two. **Run it after any change to a block's geometry.** It currently reads 1792 blocks checked, **0 disagreeing**, with four divergences named in the tool as deliberate. The most expensive bug shape on this project is an extent guessed out of a picture instead of read from the model that states it, and this is what ends it.

**`drop_showcase=1` throws one of every awkward block on the floor** in front of the spawn point, with the flat-sprite drops beside them for comparison. A dropped block is a miniature of the block itself, and nothing but looking will tell you whether a bell reads as a bell. Dropped items are never saved, so it leaves no trace.

## 5. The creature-skin situation — read this before you panic

You will find `creatures-reference.png` sitting next to `game.exe`, containing Mojang's art, plus `spawn-eggs/`, `hud-reference.png`, `font-reference.png` and `blocks-reference/` beside it. **Almost every texture you see in the running game is Mojang's.**

**This is fine. It is deliberate, it was the user's decision, and it is temporary.**

The user's own generated skins were rejected on sight, so they asked for Mojang's to go in as placeholders: *"yeah just replace all 9 textures with mojang's, i'll have my friend rework them."*

**They asked an artist friend to take the replacements on (2026-08-03).** There are two phases ahead of her and both take real time: she is **researching how UV texturing works** — how a flat image wraps onto a 3D model — and only after that comes **drawing the art itself**, which is the longer half. Expect weeks, not days. Much of `TEXTURING.md` exists to serve the first phase.

So:

- **Do not re-author the creature skins to help.** `tools/make-roster-skins.ps1` stays as a fallback and as documentation of the nets.
- **Do not lecture the user about it.** They know.
- **Do keep `TEXTURING.md` §13 (net tables) and §14 (formulas) accurate** — that is what she works from, and it is the genuinely useful contribution.
- **New species follow the same arrangement:** model it, prove it against the reference nets, leave the skin. That was confirmed as the standing choice on 2026-08-03.

**The rule that does still stand, precisely:** reference art may be **measured from**, must **never live under `assets/`**, and must **never ship in a release**. Every staging tool *refuses* to write under `assets/`, so it is mechanically enforced rather than remembered. (`SYSTEM_MEMORY.md` → "Creature skins" has which sheet rows are ours and which are covered.)

**Six placeholder sets sit beside the exe, not under `assets/`**, and they follow one arrangement:

| Beside `game.exe` | What | Restored by |
|---|---|---|
| `creatures-reference.png` | 53 of the 57 creature skins, plus the charged Bramble's energy shell and the drowned's clothing | `tools/make-reference-creature-atlas.ps1` |
| `spawn-eggs/egg00–45.png` | all 57 spawn egg sprites | `tools/make-spawn-egg-sprites.ps1` |
| `hud-reference.png` | the five catalogue tabs, over a copy of our own HUD sheet | `tools/make-reference-hud.ps1` |
| `blocks-reference/` | 663 block and item textures | `tools/make-reference-blocks.ps1` |
| `font-reference.png` | the text font, `ascii.png` copied verbatim | `tools/make-reference-font.ps1` |
| `sounds-reference/` | 497 recordings across 159 events, including 34 creature voice families and 8 music tracks | `tools/make-reference-sounds.ps1` |

`assets/textures/hud.png` is the **one exception that does live under `assets/`** — Minecraft's widget art, kept there at the user's explicit request, and also to be replaced before release.

`run.ps1` restores all six if they are missing, and **rebuilds each atlas whenever the sheet it was composited from is newer**. Do not remove that — a stale atlas serves old art silently, and it once shipped a mangled sheep through a rebuild, a re-run and a verification pass. A missing egg sprite falls back to blank rather than being skipped, because the list index is the layer index.

**The same rule covers sound**, added at M22 at the user's explicit direction: _"just use whatever sound has been placed inside reference, use mojang's noises and music and all. i'll download some kind of music editor later and make custom tracks later."_ The recordings are staged beside the exe and never under `assets/`; a missing folder makes the game run silently rather than fail.

**None of this produces a startup warning, deliberately.** Warn about *faults* — a sheet whose dimensions disagree with the code, a missing sprite, a layer constant that has drifted. Never warn about a state the user chose.

**The sequence that produced the HUD atlas is the standing rule for art, not a one-off:** stage the reference first, prove the layout against pixels known to be right, *then* author ours. Authoring art and judging the layout by it at the same time leaves two unknowns behind one symptom — the same trap as debugging a box net and a skin together.

---

## 6. Building a creature model — the procedure that stopped the failures

Three models in a row came out wrong before this was written down. Follow it in order; **each step's failure mode is invisible to the next**.

1. **Alpha runs per row, before island detection.** Touching nets merge into one island and will mislead you. The net arithmetic then falls straight out — see `TEXTURING.md` §14.1.
2. **A band narrower than predicted is information, not an error.** It means one rect is transparent, and *which one* tells you where the box is buried.
3. **Where the arithmetic ties, sample the colour.** This has settled three ambiguities that geometry could not — the cow's udder, the goat's ruff, and whether the frog's two identical nets were head-and-body (they are back-and-belly).
4. **Scan for shared extents before rendering.** Every creature quad is double-sided, so two overlapping boxes sharing any extent will z-fight, and the symptom is a flickering *triangle diagonal* that looks nothing like a modelling error. Fix by **growing the box carrying the artwork** by +0.01, never by insetting the one in front.
5. **Two renders, then your eye.** A third render means the **pose** is wrong, not the numbers. Use `creature_showcase` (§4).

**The trap that has cost the most time:** the reference happily butts boxes together with **coincident faces**, because Minecraft never draws the inward side of a surface. We do. So copying a model's exact offsets reproduces a flicker the original doesn't have — and **resizing the part cannot fix it** (bigger bulges, equal flickers, smaller looks recessed). Match the sizes and *offset* the box a sixteenth of a texel instead. `TEXTURING.md` §14.5b. **Two boxes that merely *touch* have the same problem**, and the shared-extent scan in step 4 does not catch it: overlap them slightly with different `grow` values rather than letting their faces meet.

**And check every UV against the texture's alpha before rendering.** Our reference art is Java's while the geometry is Bedrock's, and for most mobs the two sheets agree — but not all of them. A rect that comes back partly transparent means the origin is wrong; one that comes back empty means the part will silently not exist at all. The dolphin lost its entire back half to exactly this.

**The metrics are evidence, not proof.** A deliberately flattened pig once *beat* the correct one on every measure, and the user spotted four faults in seconds. The table catches gross deviation; the eye is the gate.

---

## 7. The one bug shape that keeps recurring

> **A value derived somewhere other than the one table that owns it.**

Block shapes, creature nets, sheet dimensions, knockback — each has exactly one home. Every bug in this project that "compiled and looked plausible but was subtly wrong" traces back to a second copy.

It bites hardest when you *widen* what something can be: adding slabs broke collision resolution, the fluid update, the targeting outline and the raycast, one at a time, because each had its own idea of a block's shape. **When widening an invariant, grep for the old literals** — the compiler cannot help, because nothing changed type.

**Its meanest form is a rule that is written down, correct, commented — and only in one of the two places that need it.** Lava's pooling test was water's rule minus the one clause that made water right. The player fell through unloaded chunks and was buried by them for twenty milestones while creatures, guarded against exactly that since the day they were written, never did. Neither is a *missing* rule you could grep for; both are a rule that exists and did not travel. **When you write a guard, ask what else does the same thing.**

---

## 8. Things that are settled — do not re-litigate

- **C++20, Vulkan, GLFW, CMake + Ninja, FetchContent.** Each was chosen deliberately; `CLAUDE.md` has the reasoning.
- **No multiplayer, ever.** It is a design freedom, not a limitation — do not add abstractions "in case".
- **`engine/` must never reference `game/`.**
- **Generation is a pure function of `(seed, chunkCoord)`; meshing a pure function of its input volume. Only the main thread mutates the world.** This is what makes the threading work and cannot be retrofitted.
- **The renderer was rewritten at M23** and is no longer the throwaway it used to be. Do not add abstraction layers to it either; the seven passes are concrete on purpose and there is still exactly one backend.
- **Mechanics may follow Minecraft freely; assets must be ours.** Ordinary animal names (sheep, wolf, frog) are free; only *coined* names need replacing — which is why the creeper is a **Bramble**.

---

## 9. Talking to the user

They are an experienced vibe coder but **not** a C++ or graphics programmer. Use the correct technical term, then immediately explain it in plain English — they have asked for this explicitly, as a way of learning over time. Do not substitute vague language, and do not drown them in theory either.

They think in outcomes and feel. Translate that into a technical plan yourself rather than asking them to specify one.

**When they report a bug, default to "this is real and I haven't found it yet."** Three of the four bugs at M3 were found by them playing, not by reading code. None produced a warning.
